subject: principles-of-accounts
title: Double Entry: One Purchase, Two Accounts
objectives: Describe double entry in order: opening balance, the purchase, both accounts changing by the same $4,000, the equation re-checked
Explain why total assets stay at $10,000 when cash is swapped for equipment of equal value
Use the accounting equation Assets = Capital + Liabilities to check that a transaction balances

definitions.meaning: The system in which every transaction is recorded twice, once in each of the two accounts it changes, by the same amount.
Something of value the business owns, such as its cash or its equipment.
The owner's stake in the business: the value the owner has put in, $10,000 at the opening position.
Amounts the business owes to others; $0 at the opening position in this example.
The account recording the business's cash; it falls by $4,000, from $10,000 to $6,000, when equipment is bought for cash (s3).
The account recording the business's equipment; it rises by $4,000, from $0 to $4,000, when equipment is bought for cash (s3).
An entry in an account recording value coming in or an asset rising, one side of a double-entry recording.
An entry in an account recording value going out or a claim rising, the other side of a double-entry recording.
Assets = Capital + Liabilities: the rule that total assets always equal the owner's stake plus what is owed, before and after every transaction.

mechanismSteps: Opening, equation balances: the business opens with $10,000 cash provided by the owner as capital and owes nothing, so assets of $10,000 equal capital of $10,000 plus liabilities of $0 (s1).
The purchase, two movements at once: the business pays $4,000 cash and the equipment arrives in the same transaction (s2).
Both accounts change by $4,000: cash falls by $4,000 to $6,000 and equipment rises by $4,000 to $4,000 at the same moment (s3).
Re-checked, still balances: total assets are $6,000 cash plus $4,000 equipment, still $10,000, and Assets = Capital + Liabilities still balances (s4).
workedExample: Work the purchase account by account. Step 1 (s1): the business opens with cash $10,000, capital $10,000 and liabilities $0, so total assets are $10,000. Step 2 (s2): it pays $4,000 cash for equipment. Step 3 (s3): the $4,000 swap - cash falls by $4,000 to $6,000 and equipment rises by $4,000 to $4,000 at the same moment. Step 4 (s4): cash $6,000 plus equipment $4,000 gives total assets stay at $10,000, unchanged, and Assets = Capital + Liabilities stays balanced.

trap.misconception: Buying equipment with cash makes the business poorer so total assets fall.
trap.explanation: The slip: Cash has visibly left the business, so it is easy to feel that value has been lost - money paid out reads as the business ending up with less than it had before. The fix: One asset is swapped for another of equal value, so total assets and the equation are unchanged. Paying $4,000 cash for equipment cuts the cash asset by $4,000 and raises the equipment asset by $4,000 at the same moment, total assets stay at $10,000, and Assets = Capital + Liabilities stays balanced - every transaction is recorded twice, once in each account it changes. In class, replay scene 3: freeze on both accounts changing together and ask where the $4,000 went - it is sitting in the equipment account, which is why total assets are unchanged even though the cash balance fell.
